newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Canberra envoy headed for Cambodia despite tension.
newsitem.headline: Canberra envoy headed for Cambodia despite tension.

text.p: Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said on Saturday that Canberra would proceed with its plan to send a special envoy to Cambodia at the weekend despite fresh clashes between troops loyal to the country's rival prime ministers.

"I am becoming increasingly concerned about the situation in Cambodia and that is clearly a concern that is shared by other countries in the region and beyond," Downer told a news conference in Hanoi.
He said the safety of Australians living in Cambodia was his government's priority and a crisis group had been set up in Canberra for that to be ensured.

However, he said it was important for John Dauth, First Assistant Secretary of the South and Southeast Asia Division in the Foreign Ministry, to proceed with his trip to the Cambodian capital on Sunday.
Downer said earlier this week that Dauth would "convey Australian government concerns to the highest levels of government" in Cambodia over tensions in the Southeast Asian nation.

"Clearly, if things deteriorated to the point where it would become unsafe for Mr. Dauth...he wouldn't be able to go. But as things stand I think it's important that he does proceed with his mission," Downer said.
A military official loyal to Cambodian First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said rival government troops clashed on the outskirts of Phnom Penh on Saturday.

The clash came as radio controlled by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) broadcast a warning from defence and security officials that searches were under way for "illegal troops" and weapons in the city.
Hun Sen warned earlier this week that Ranariddh's soldiers were bringing Khmer Rouge guerrilla defectors into the city illegally. Ranariddh has denied moving troops into the city.
Both prime ministers were out of the country on Saturday, their offices said, but their exact whereabouts could not be immediately confirmed.
Reuters reported from neighbouring Thailand that the airport in Phnom Penh was closed on Saturday and at least one flight was forced to return to Bangkok.

Downer noted that donor nations meeting in Paris this week had pledged aid of $450 million for Cambodia in 1997/98, but not without expressing concern about the country's deteriorating political situation.

"And so we're at a point now where the international community is making very strong representations about the situation on the ground in Cambodia, and we hope that the parties in Cambodia will respond positively to those representations," he said.
